# Paired maximum-depth equality rigidity in dimensions at least three

## Theorem and definitions

Let d≥3, let K⊂R^d be a convex body, let V=|K|>0, and put
Γ_d=(d/(d+1))^d. For y∈K define

    p_K(y)= inf_(u≠0,s∈R)
       [ |K∩{x:u·(x−y)≥s}|+|K∩{x:u·(x−y)≥−s}| ]/(2V),
    D_pair(K)=max_(y∈K) p_K(y).

Then the maximum exists, D_pair(K)≥Γ_d, and

    D_pair(K)=Γ_d    if and only if K is a simplex.            (R)

A key equality refinement, valid for every such body with centroid g, is

    |K∩{u·(x−g)≥s}|+|K∩{u·(x−g)≥−s}| > 2Γ_d V             (E)

for every u≠0 and every s≠0. Thus an equality pair at the centroid has
zero shift and is an ordinary Grünbaum equality cap.

This is an ordinary continuous theorem. It asserts no mixed-integer
center, no compatibility-preserving fiber deformation, and no result
for d=2. The complete paired centroid lower bound is already proved in
`candidate 732b11a769399016`; the strictness
and rigidity steps are proved below.

## 1. Precise attained localization input

We use the standard one-constraint localization theorem, Theorem 2 of
Fradelizi–Guédon (2004), independently checked in the
[author-uploaded full text](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220452814_The_Extreme_Points_of_Subsets_of_s_-Concave_Probabilities_and_a_Geometric_Localization_Theorem).
For σ≤1/2, on a fixed compact convex support, a convex upper
semicontinuous functional on σ-concave probabilities subject to one
upper semicontinuous integral inequality attains its supremum at an
admissible Dirac or a σ-affine segment law saturating the constraint.
The paper explicitly proves compactness and attainment; it is not only
a reduction to an unclosed family of candidate laws.

Fix a compact interval I, d≥3, and s>0. Among 1/d-concave probabilities
ν supported in I with ∫x dν≥0, maximize

    Φ_s(ν)=ν((−∞,−s])+ν((−∞,s]).                             (1)

This functional is affine and weakly upper semicontinuous by the closed
set form of Portmanteau; the mean constraint is continuous on I. The
localization theorem therefore supplies an actual maximizing extremizer.
Its possible forms are:

- a Dirac at x≥0, for which Φ_s≤1;
- a nondegenerate centered segment law whose density is proportional to
  a nonnegative affine function to power d−1.

The extra one-sided moment condition in the localization theorem imposes
no additional candidates: a centered nondegenerate segment law has strictly
negative proper initial moments and strictly positive proper final moments.

In Sections 2–3 we prove that EVERY listed extremizer has

    Φ_s < 2−2Γ_d.                                           (2)

Because a maximizing extremizer exists on this FIXED compact interval,
(2) gives a strict bound for the supremum itself. This is the crucial
attainment step: no uniform gap over an unclosed parameter family is
being inferred merely from its pointwise strict inequalities.

## 2. Strict affine-power bounds: all decreasing branches

An increasing nonconstant affine-power density, after an increasing affine
change of variable, has the normalized form

    f_(d,r)(t)=d t^(d−1)/(1−r^d),       r≤t≤1, 0≤r<1.

Its mean and distribution function are denoted by m and G. Direct integration
and pairing about the interval midpoint give

    m=[d/(d+1)](1−r^(d+1))/(1−r^d),
    (1+r)/2≤m<1.

For h≥0 set H(h)=G(m−h)+G(m+h). On 0<h≤1−m, both arguments belong
to [r,1] and

    H'(h)=f_(d,r)(m+h)−f_(d,r)(m−h)>0.

On 1−m≤h≤m−r, the upper distribution function is one, so H(h)≥1.
For h≥m−r it is exactly one. The ordinary Grünbaum inequality applied
to the actual convex frustum {(t,w):r≤t≤1,w∈tL}, where L is any
(d−1)-dimensional convex body, gives G(m)≥Γ_d. Consequently

    H(h)>2Γ_d       for EVERY h>0.                            (3)

Indeed it strictly increases from H(0)≥2Γ_d on the first interval,
and is at least one thereafter, while Γ_d<1/2.

Reflection of a centered increasing affine-power law gives the decreasing
case. Atomlessness makes its paired lower-CDF sum exactly 2−H(h), with
h>0 corresponding to the original fixed s>0. Equation (3) proves (2)
for every decreasing nonconstant extremizer. A constant affine root gives
a centered uniform interval, whose paired lower-CDF sum is one; this is
also strictly below 2−2Γ_d. The Dirac case from §1 is strict for the same
reason.

## 3. Strict affine-power bounds: all increasing branches

The preceding monotonicity also gives the exact upper envelope

    max_(h≥0) H(h)=1+T_d(r),
    T_d(r)=[(2m−1)^d−r^d]/(1−r^d).                          (4)

The maximum occurs at h=1−m: the lower argument is still in support,
then H decreases until it reaches one. We prove T_d(r)<1−2Γ_d.

For d=3 put A=1+r+r², N=A+3r³. Then 2m−1=N/(2A), and direct
polynomial multiplication gives

    (5+27r³)A³−4N³=(1−r)P(r),
    P(r)=1+4r+10r²+8r³+23r⁴+80r⁵+90r⁶+108r⁷+81r⁸.

Hence

    1−2Γ_3−T_3(r)=5/32−T_3(r)=P(r)/(32A⁴)>0.               (5)

Every factor is explicit and positive for 0≤r<1. Thus no endpoint
r=0 or nearly degenerate interval is an omitted equality case.

For completeness, the dimension-independent estimate used for d≥4 is
T_d(r)≤1/6. Here is the scalar proof. For 0<v≤1 define

    J(v)=−log v−(1−v)(7+5v)/[2(1+5v)].

Its derivative is (v−1)(5v−1)(5v−2)/[2v(1+5v)²]. Its only possible
minima are at v=1 and v=1/5; J tends to infinity at zero. One has
J(1)=0 and J(1/5)=log5−8/5>0. The last inequality follows exactly from

    log5=2Σ_(j≥0) (2/3)^(2j+1)/(2j+1)
        >2Σ_(j=0)^3 (2/3)^(2j+1)/(2j+1)>8/5.

Now fix 0≤Q<1 and put a=(1+5Q)/6. Substitution
v=(Q+t)/(1+t), t>0, in J(v)≥0 gives

    1/(1+t)+1/(a+t)
      ≤ [2/(1−Q)]∫_Q^1 du/(u+t).                            (6)

Multiplying by t and using u/(u+t)=1−t/(u+t), this is equivalent to

    1/(1+t)+a/(a+t)
      ≥ [2/(1−Q)]∫_Q^1 u/(u+t) du.

For 0<α<1 use the positive integral representation

    u^α=C_α∫_0^∞ t^(α−1)u/(u+t) dt,
    C_α=[∫_0^∞ t^(α−1)/(1+t) dt]^(−1)>0.

Scaling proves the identity, including u=0. Each integral is finite;
Tonelli justifies averaging before integration. Thus (6) gives

    [2/(1−Q)]∫_Q^1 u^α du ≤ 1+[(1+5Q)/6]^α.

Take α=1/d and Q=r^d. The average on the left is 2m, so
(2m−1)^d≤(1+5r^d)/6. Since 2m−1≥r≥0, taking powers preserves
the inequality and (4) gives T_d(r)≤1/6.

Finally Γ_d is decreasing in d, as follows by differentiating
−d log(1+1/d) and using log(1+x)>x/(1+x). Therefore, for d≥4,

    1−2Γ_d−T_d(r)
       ≥1−2Γ_4−1/6=53/3750>0.                              (7)

Equations (4)–(7) prove (2) for every increasing extremizer. This completes
the strict localization argument of §1.

## 4. Transfer to every actual centroid marginal

For a convex body K and u≠0, the law of u·(X−g), with X uniform on K,
is compactly supported, centered, and atomless. Its density has concave
1/(d−1) power by Brunn–Minkowski; equivalently its measure concavity
parameter is 1/d. Thus it is an admissible law in §1 on some fixed
compact interval containing its support.

At both thresholds its atomless closed upper and lower tails are
complementary. Therefore (2) translates exactly into (E). Negative s
is the same pair with its terms exchanged. At s=0 the ordinary centroid
inequality gives the nonstrict lower bound 2Γ_dV. In particular p_K(g)≥Γ_d.
All cap boundaries have d-volume zero, even at support endpoints.

## 5. Compact paired extrema and balancing of the active normals

Translate g to zero for this section. Choose R>0 with K⊂RB_2^d. Normalize
u to unit length and replace s by |s|; this does not change the infimum.
For every y∈K, every |u|=1 and every s≥2R, one cap is empty up to a
volume-null support hyperplane and the other contains K. Their average
fraction is 1/2. Thus the infimum defining p_K(y) is exactly a minimum
on the fixed compact parameter space

    Q=S^(d−1)×[0,2R].

The paired cap function P(y,u,s) is jointly continuous on K×Q by dominated
convergence: its two boundary hyperplanes always have zero volume.
Consequently p_K is continuous and attains its maximum on compact K.
The centroid lower bound makes this maximum positive. Boundary points
have zero depth using s=0 and a supporting cap, so all maximizers are
interior points.

Assume now D_pair(K)=Γ_d. Then p_K(g)=Γ_d. By (E), its compact active
set is exactly

    {(u,0):u∈U},
    U={|u|=1:|K∩{u·(x−g)≥0}|/V=Γ_d}.

The set U is nonempty and compact. We claim 0∈conv(U). If not, strict
separation gives v and a>0 such that u·v≥a for every u∈U. Take r>0
with g+rB_2^d⊂K and the parameter neighborhood

    N={(u,s)∈Q:u·v>a/2, s<r/4}.

It contains the entire active set. On its compact complement, P(g,u,s)
is at least Γ_d+b for some b>0.

Move the actual candidate to y_t=g−tv, with t>0 small enough that
t|v|<r/4. On N, each of the thresholds ±s is lowered by t u·v≥ta/2.
All intervening sections lie within signed distance r/2 of g. The inner
ball gives a uniform positive lower bound c for their normalized
(d−1)-section areas, so the paired average gains at least cta/2.
Its starting value was at least Γ_d. On Q\N, an outer ball gives a
uniform upper bound L for normalized section area, so threshold movement
changes the paired average by at most Lt|v|. Taking t small enough that
Lt|v|<b/2 makes every such pair exceed Γ_d+b/2.

Thus EVERY parameter in Q gives mass strictly above Γ_d at y_t, with a
uniform positive minimum gap. The point y_t remains in int K. This
contradicts D_pair(K)=Γ_d and proves 0∈conv(U). No unproved derivative
envelope formula or exchange of an unattained infimum was used.

## 6. Balanced ordinary equality caps force a simplex

By Carathéodory, select distinct u_1,...,u_k∈U and positive θ_i,
k≤d+1, with Σθ_i u_i=0. The classical equality case of the ordinary
Grünbaum inequality says that each equality direction represents K as a
pyramid conv(v_i,F_i), with its equality cap on the apex side. Let λ_i
be its affine height, zero on F_i and one at v_i. Then λ_i≥0 on K,
its gradient is a positive multiple of u_i, and its volume mean is
1/(d+1), by integrating the pyramid sections proportional to
(1−t)^(d−1).

Every extreme point other than v_i lies in F_i: intermediate heights
lie on a nontrivial segment between the apex and the base. Distinct
u_i have distinct apices, because for a fixed apex the other extreme
points span and determine its full (d−1)-dimensional base hyperplane.
Therefore λ_i(v_j)=δ_ij.

Rescale the positive θ_i to positive β_i so that Σβ_i grad λ_i=0.
The function Σβ_i λ_i is constant. Evaluating at v_j shows that this
constant equals every β_j, and is positive. Consequently Σλ_i=1.
Integrating gives k/(d+1)=1, hence k=d+1. The identities λ_i(v_j)=δ_ij
make the apices affinely independent. The inequalities λ_i≥0 and
Σλ_i=1 place K inside their simplex, while convexity gives the reverse
inclusion. Thus K is a simplex.

Conversely, for a simplex some barycentric coordinate of any y is at
least 1/(d+1). Its facet-parallel apex cap has fraction at most Γ_d.
Using that cap with s=0 gives p_K(y)≤Γ_d at every y. The centroid paired
bound gives equality there. This proves (R).

## 7. A compact ordinary stability corollary and dimensional scope

For two normalized finite measures, the paired-depth functions at every
ambient candidate differ by at most total variation: each of the two
cap differences is at most that amount, and they are averaged. Infima
and then suprema preserve this bound. For uniform convex bodies, points
outside the body have paired depth zero by choosing s=0 and a separating
cap, so the ambient supremum is the same as the maximum over the body.

Hence D_pair is continuous under Hausdorff convergence of bodies containing
a fixed ball and contained in a fixed ball, by their normalized total
variation convergence. The compact normalized class at a fixed positive
Hausdorff distance from all simplices therefore has an attained strictly
positive gap above Γ_d, by (R). This is a qualitative compact gap, with
no claim of a uniform dimensional constant or mixed compatibility.

The argument deliberately excludes d=2: the increasing triangular density
at mean 2/3 and shift 1/3 attains paired tail sum 8/9=2Γ_2. Nonzero-shift
active pairs cannot be removed by (E) in that dimension. For d=1 every
convex body is an interval; the classification is trivial, but nonzero
shifts can again be equality pairs. Neither case is silently included
in the strict statement (E).
